notes: Asbatankvoy demurrage and shifting appeal; breakdown of equipment and clause 9 construction are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Asbatankvoy demurrage: breakdown of consignee equipment at Dakar sealine
key_facts: Owners claimed demurrage and shifting expenses after the tanker Afrapearl discharged fuel oil at Dakar under an amended Asbatankvoy voyage charterparty.
Discharge at the M'bao sealine was repeatedly interrupted by leaks from a corroded pipeline flange operated by consignee SAR.
The judge held owners entitled to full demurrage and additional agency fees under clauses 8 and 9.
Charterers appealed on whether delay was caused by a breakdown of consignee equipment under clause 8 and whether repeated shifts off the berth triggered clause 9.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from arbitration award on demurrage and additional agency fees under an Asbatankvoy voyage charterparty.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on both issues; owners entitled only to half demurrage for the disputed period and not to additional agency fees under clause 9.
enrichment.ratio: Under Asbatankvoy clause 8, a malfunction of consignee pipeline equipment that prevents discharge constitutes a breakdown of equipment even if caused by prior neglect, but half demurrage does not apply where the breakdown was caused by charterers' fault; clause 9 covers shifting between discharge berths and does not extend to orders to leave a berth for repairs at the same berth.
legal_issues: Whether a gap in a consignee sealine flange amounted to a breakdown of equipment under clause 8
Whether pre-existing pipeline defects precluded a breakdown within the meaning of the charter
Whether delay was caused by the breakdown or by failure to repair earlier
Whether repeated movements off and on the same berth were shifting between berths under clause 9

Reardon Smith Line v Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food [1962] 1 QB 42

notes: Farmer negligence for straying cattle on public footpath gate; foreseeability and duty of care analysis is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Farmer liable for cattle straying through footpath gate onto road
key_facts: Cattle belonging to farmer Mr Wilson strayed onto the B1257 near Middlesbrough after walkers left open a gate on a public footpath through his upper field.
The cattle passed through neglected Home Farm land with unfenced access to the road, a situation known to Wilson and his son.
The county court recorder found it foreseeable that careless walkers would leave the gate open and that cattle could reach the highway.
Wilson had relied on a hook-and-chain gate secured by the National Park Authority rather than self-closing gates, stiles, kissing-gates, or a cattle grid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Middlesbrough County Court finding farmer liable in negligence for road accident caused by straying cattle.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; farmer held negligent for failing to take reasonable precautions against cattle escaping via the footpath gate.
enrichment.ratio: Where a farmer grazes cattle in a field separated from a road only by a heavily used right-of-way and known dilapidated fencing on adjoining land, he owes a duty to guard against the foreseeable carelessness of lawful walkers who may leave a stock gate open; absence of prior incidents does not negate foreseeability when the contemporary risk is clear.
legal_issues: Whether leaving a footpath gate unsecured was negligent given 36 years without prior straying
Whether additional gate security measures were required as a matter of reasonable foresight
Whether expert evidence on general farming practice was necessary
Application of Animals Act 1971 section 8 abolishing common law immunity for straying livestock
linked_authorities: Searle v Wallbank [1947] AC 341

confidence.notes: Recorder's findings and Court of Appeal reasoning on foreseeability and duty are clear. Policy implications for farmers nationwide were debated but not decisive.

notes: Animal rights nuisance call sentencing appeal; reduced sentences and harassment Act comparison are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Reduced sentences for animal rights nuisance telephone campaign
key_facts: Holliday and Leboutillier pleaded guilty to causing a public nuisance through over 1,000 nuisance telephone calls to Covance Laboratories, Huntingdon Life Sciences, and individuals connected with animal testing.
Neither defendant sent letter bombs in a contemporaneous campaign, but Leboutillier made threatening calls referencing bombs and death threats.
Holliday's calls were primarily switchboard jamming without bomb references; he had pleaded guilty nearly a year before sentencing.
Judge Hoffman sentenced Holliday to 18 months and Leboutillier to five years imprisonment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for leave to appeal against sentence for public nuisance arising from animal rights telephone harassment.
enrichment.outcome: Sentences reduced to nine months for Holliday and 30 months for Leboutillier; court commended harassment Act prosecution where appropriate.
enrichment.ratio: Sentences for public nuisance in animal rights telephone campaigns must reflect the absence of violence, property damage, and repeated victimisation; where section 2 harassment would have capped Holliday's sentence at six months, a nine-month public nuisance sentence was appropriate, and Leboutillier's five-year term was manifestly excessive compared with Schilling and Harley.
legal_issues: Whether 18 months and five years were manifestly excessive for public nuisance telephone calls
Appropriate starting points where defendants had no connection to letter bomb campaign
Whether prosecution under Protection from Harassment Act 1997 was preferable
Credit for guilty pleas and mental health mitigation for Holliday
linked_authorities: R v Schilling [2002] EWCA Crim 3198
R v Harley [2002] EWCA Crim 2650

notes: Fresh asylum claim and NASS support under section 94; academic claim but point of general importance clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Fresh asylum claim does not automatically trigger continuing NASS support
key_facts: Ethiopian claimant Nigatu's asylum claim and appeals were rejected; he submitted further medical and membership evidence said to constitute a fresh claim.
NASS notified removal of asylum support 28 days after final appeal rejection, before the Home Office decided whether the further representations amounted to a fresh claim.
Richards J had indicated that post-adjudicator medical evidence could support further representations to the Secretary of State.
The Secretary of State later accepted the claim as a fresh claim and support was continued under an interim order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, rendered academic as to the claimant but pursued to decide a point of general importance on asylum support eligibility.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on the merits; making further representations asserted to be a fresh claim does not automatically make the person an asylum seeker entitled to section 95 support until the Secretary of State records it as a fresh claim.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 94 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, a person is an asylum seeker only when a claim has been recorded by the Secretary of State and not determined; after an initial claim is exhausted, further representations do not trigger support until the Secretary of State decides they constitute a fresh claim, with section 4 providing a safety net against destitution.
legal_issues: Whether submitting further asylum representations after exhausted appeals automatically restores asylum seeker status for support purposes
Construction of 'recorded' in section 94 compared with initial claims
Application of R v SSHD ex parte Onibiyo to support under Part 6
Whether NASS should coordinate with casework branches when fresh claims are pending
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Onibiyo [1996] QB 768
Limbuela v Secretary of State [2004] EWCA Civ 540
Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and Onibiyo analysis are detailed. Claim was academic for the individual claimant but the legal point is clearly resolved.

notes: Mental capacity and CT scan under general anaesthesia; uncontested application with clear medical evidence.

enrichment.short_title: CT scan under general anaesthesia authorised for incapacitated psychiatric patient
key_facts: Elderly patient C with paranoid schizophrenia refused investigation of a suspected left renal carcinoma found on ultrasound after haematuria.
C lacked insight, believed scans were substituted, and regarded medical treatment as part of a plot against her.
Psychiatrists concluded she lacked capacity to decide on physical health treatment; a CT scan was essential to stage the tumour.
The Official Solicitor did not oppose the NHS Trust application for a declaration permitting general anaesthesia and restraint if necessary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by NHS Trust for declaration that CT scan under general anaesthesia against patient's wishes was lawful.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted with consent order; CT scan held to be in C's best interests given lack of capacity.
enrichment.ratio: Where a detained psychiatric patient lacks capacity because paranoid delusions prevent her weighing treatment information, and medical evidence unanimously shows a CT scan is essential to investigate probable renal malignancy, the court may authorise examination under general anaesthesia as being in her best interests.
legal_issues: Whether C lacked capacity to consent to investigation of suspected renal carcinoma
Whether CT scan under general anaesthesia was in the patient's best interests
Lawfulness of physical restraint to administer anaesthesia
Interaction between Mental Health Act detention and treatment of physical illness

notes: Planning appeal on Article 8 proportionality at Bankside; extensive HRA analysis with appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Bankside planning permission: Article 8 and loss of residential amenity
key_facts: First Secretary of State granted planning permission for a 20-storey redevelopment between Blackfriars Bridge and Southwark Bridge near Tate Modern.
Residents of Bankside Lofts and Falcon Point objected to loss of daylight, privacy, views, television reception, and property value.
The Inspector found breach of Southwark UDP Policy E3.1 on amenity but justified departure for regeneration benefits.
Collins J refused judicial review; residents appealed solely on Human Rights Act grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of judicial review of planning permission granted on appeal by the Secretary of State.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no breach of Article 8 or Article 1 Protocol 1; Samaroo two-stage proportionality test not required in competing private land-use context.
enrichment.ratio: Article 8 does not create an absolute right to existing residential amenities; in planning decisions involving competing landowner and community interests, a conventional balancing of material considerations satisfies proportionality, and diminution in property value alone does not constitute a separate Convention breach.
legal_issues: Whether loss of daylight, privacy, and views engaged Article 8
Whether the Inspector erred by failing to apply explicit proportionality analysis
Whether Samaroo two-stage test applied to planning appeals
Whether property value diminution was a separate breach of Article 1 Protocol 1

enrichment.short_title: Civil recovery of cocaine-linked cash: diamond-laundering defence rejected
key_facts: About £3.5 million in cash seized from Charrington in 1992 was linked to laundering proceeds of large-scale cocaine importations masterminded by Curtis Warren.
Charrington had acted as police informant but admitted laundering drug money; prosecution was later dropped after Warren's acquittal.
The Assets Recovery Agency sought summary judgment; Charrington claimed the cash was lawful commission from diamond sales.
Collins J rejected Charrington's account as incredible but adjourned Warren's defence for further Customs enquiries.

enrichment.outcome: Summary judgment granted against Charrington with costs; Warren's application adjourned to allow targeted document enquiries.
enrichment.ratio: Where seized cash was contaminated with cocaine and contemporaneous admissions and records point to drug-money laundering, a late claim that the funds represent lawful diamond commission lacks any real prospect of success and warrants summary judgment under CPR 24.2.

notes: Supplemental judgment on Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal power to impose practice conditions under section 47.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors Tribunal must impose its own practice conditions on suspension
key_facts: Following Camacho's successful appeal reducing indefinite suspension to 18 months, the court had imposed five conditions on his return to practice.
The Law Society and Tribunal argued conditions should be recommendations for practising certificates rather than Tribunal orders.
Section 47 gives the Tribunal broad power to make such orders as it thinks fit on disciplinary applications.
The court rejected delegation and confirmed the Tribunal may impose indefinite conditions with permission to apply to vary.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplemental judgment following appeal in Camacho v Law Society on scope of Tribunal powers to impose conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Court confirmed Tribunal power to impose conditions directly; rejected Law Society arguments for recommendation-only practice; case management observations on Tribunal procedure not withdrawn.
enrichment.ratio: Section 47 of the Solicitors Act 1974 empowers the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal itself to impose conditions restricting practice as part of a suspension penalty; the Tribunal should not delegate that public protection task to the Law Society, which is not bound by recommendations and exercises separate regulatory powers over practising certificates.
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal has power under section 47 to impose conditions on practice
Whether conditions should be recommendations to the Law Society instead
Whether conditions may run indefinitely with permission to apply to vary
Who polices and enforces Tribunal conditions on return to practice

notes: FOS time-bar refusal upheld on permission to appeal; ombudsman jurisdiction and fairness points clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Financial Ombudsman time-bar on retirement endowment complaint upheld
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Ropaigealach took a 20-year endowment mortgage package from MGM in January 1990.
They complained to MGM in September 2000 about unsuitability; MGM rejected the complaint in October 2001.
A complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service was made in April 2002; the ombudsman held the retirement-related complaint time-barred by July 2002.
Sullivan J refused permission for judicial review; the applicants did not appear at the Court of Appeal hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against refusal of permission to seek judicial review of Financial Ombudsman decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no real prospect of success on time-bar point or alleged procedural unfairness.
enrichment.ratio: Where a mortgage endowment complaint that the policy extended into retirement was known from inception, the ombudsman correctly held it time-barred under analogous six-year limitation principles; clarifying the time-bar with the firm, declining an oral hearing while allowing written representations, and refusing post-decision internal guidance were not procedurally unfair.

Whether it was unfair to ask MGM whether to take a time-bar point
Whether denial of an oral hearing was procedurally unfair
Whether MGM should have disclosed internal guidance after the final decision

notes: Attorney General reference on unduly lenient manslaughter sentence; increased to nine years with public protection analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient manslaughter sentence increased to nine years
key_facts: Defendant pleaded guilty to manslaughter on an indictment for murder after killing partner Kelly Reid during a drunken fight in July 2003.
A Newton hearing found death caused by chest compression and non-consensual anal penetration by the defendant.
Judge Roberts sentenced six years plus 137 days consecutive from an earlier unexpired term.
The defendant had 27 previous convictions including repeated violent offences against men but none for domestic violence against women.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging unduly lenient sentence for manslaughter.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; sentence quashed and substituted with nine years' imprisonment as a longer-than-commensurate term for public protection; consecutive return order quashed.
enrichment.ratio: For no-intent manslaughter with contested facts at a Newton hearing and a serious non-fatal sexual assault, a commensurate sentence of seven to eight years was appropriate and section 80(2)(b) required a longer term of about ten years before double jeopardy adjustment, given the offender's persistent violent record and inability to control violent instincts when drunk.
legal_issues: Whether six years was unduly lenient for no-intent manslaughter with sexual assault
Whether section 80(2)(b) required a longer-than-commensurate sentence for public protection
Appropriate credit for guilty plea where facts were disputed at Newton hearing
Relevance of prior violence record where victims were male not female

R v Tzambazales [1997] 1 Cr App R(S) 87
Attorney General's References Nos 74, 95 and 115 of 2002 [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 42
